entries.text: The town's coin. Taxes, rents and trade fill the treasury; bounties, buildings, wages and upkeep empty it. A treasury that runs dry can't pay the watch or the sellswords.
What a loaf costs in gold. It climbs when food runs short and falls when the farms and granaries are full. Dear bread sours the townsfolk and costs you Mandate.
Grown on farmland and stored in cellars and granaries for the winter. Too little and the price of bread climbs; none at all and people go hungry.
Cut by woodcutters and used for nearly every building, the palisade and furniture.
Made by smiths from stone and timber. Workshops and builders use them up.
Brewed from barley and hops. Taverns pour it, and a town with ale is a happier one, and draws adventurers.
Quarried for townhouses, stone walls, towers and grand works.
Shorn from flocks on pasture and spun into cloth by weavers.
Woven from wool. Households want it, and it sells well to caravans.
Made from timber by carpenters. Better houses want it before they grow another storey.
Grown in herb beds. Healers and alchemists brew them into potions.
Brewed from herbs. Heroes buy them before they set out, and they save lives in a hard fight.
Pressed from vineyards. Wealthy households want it, and it is a fine gift for an envoy.
Copied by scribes. Scholars and the library want them, and wealthy households read them.

Everything the town makes and uses besides coin: food, timber, tools, ale, stone, wool, cloth, furniture, herbs, potions, wine and books. A trade route sells your surplus and brings back what you are short of.
What the town pays every day to keep things running: the watch's wages, buildings, patronage and sellswords. It comes out of the treasury.
The families living in town. A household is a few souls under one roof. Charters ask for a number of households, and each one pays taxes and rent.
Every person in town counted one by one: a rough reckoning from the households.
Townsfolk with no roof. Paint more residential zones so homes go up, or the homeless sour the town and some will leave.
How much the townsfolk back you, out of 100. Cheap bread, signing the motions they want and winning wars raise it; hunger, high taxes and defeats lower it. A mayor whose Mandate runs out falls.

What the town is chartered as: thorp, hamlet, village, town, large town, city and great city. The City window shows what the next charter asks for: households, institutions, sometimes walls, and gold. Each new charter opens buildings, wards and density.
Ground you paint for a use: residential, commercial, industry or farmland. You don't place houses: the townsfolk build in your zones as they can afford to, facing the lanes that wear in.

A district of the town with its own character and voice: the Market Ward favours shops, the Trades Ward workshops, Castle Hill manors. Land outside your wards can't be zoned. Wards like or dislike your choices.
How tightly a zone is built: low, medium (from the town charter) or high (from the large town charter). Dense land grows townhouses and tall houses and sells dearer, but crowds its people a little.
Paths wear in by themselves along the routes people walk most, and buildings go up facing them. Decorations and buildings are walked around.
Trees, benches, lamps, fountains, statues and more, set anywhere at any angle. Each helps a little: houses on a pleasant street are more content and grow sooner, and the land nearby sells dearer.
How happy a household is with its home: food, goods, safety, neighbours and a pleasant street. Content households grow their houses another storey.
How strongly the town draws settlers: jobs, homes, cheap bread, low taxes, safety and fame. The City window breaks it down.
The food laid by in cellars and granaries to last the winter. If they run short, buy grain from the traders before the snow.
Great projects such as a clock tower, an aqueduct or a mage tower, unlocked charter by charter. One rises over seasons, drawing gold and goods for each stage, and helps the whole town once it stands.

The civic heart of the town: the temple district, the adventurers' hall, the druid grove, the grand bazaar, the famous tavern. Each has a keeper, does something for the town every day, and asks you for things now and then.
How generously the council funds an institution: unfunded, modest or generous. More patronage buys more of its service and its keeper's goodwill.
The cellars, sewers and catacombs under the streets. Each charter opens a deeper level. Left alone a level stirs until something comes up at night; patrols and bounties keep it quiet.
The year turns: summer brings visitors and war bands, autumn the harvest, winter empty fields, snowbound roads and the hungry dead.
The ordinary people of the town. They work, trade, drink and gossip, and are trained only in their own trade. Heroes are better at most things.
Adventurers who come to town for work. You don't command them: you post bounties, and they choose what to take on. Reward, knight or honour them to keep them loyal.
A band of adventurers who travel and fight together under one name. Companies take bounties, explore, sell reports of what they found and, once famous, raise bastions.
The heroes out on one job together. Once a party leaves town it is lost in the fog until it reports or sends word.
How firmly a hero is bound to the town. Pay, gifts, honours and choices they approve of raise it. Loyal heroes stay when times turn dark; disloyal ones leave, or go over to the enemy.
What a hero values: merciful, ruthless, pious, mercenary, lawful, free-spirited or bold. Your choices please or anger them by it, and that moves their loyalty.
A good name. Clearing ruins, helping villages and holding the walls earn it. Famous heroes draw others to town and frighten the foe, but want more for a bounty.
A bad name, earned by brawls, theft, desertion and treachery. The council won't knight the notorious, and their past tends to catch up with them.
A name the bards give a famous hero, like "the Unbowed".
A lasting part a hero takes in the town, such as the tavern's bard or a paladin sworn to it. It helps the town every day while the hero stays loyal.
The hero you name to stand for the town. A champion is honoured above the others and is first to answer when the town is threatened.
A hero who has gone over to the enemy. Disloyal and infamous heroes are the likeliest to turn.
A keep a famous company raises on the edge of town, with facilities like a smithy or a drill yard. It hires townsfolk, and its sentries stand on the walls in a siege.
Three councillors who bring motions for you to sign or veto. You set taxes and the watch with them. A council that stops listening is how mayors fall.
A proposal a councillor brings to you. Sign it or veto it; one left alone passes on its own when its time runs out.
A law in force for a while, such as lifted tolls or a curfew. Decrees come from motions and from your answers to petitions.
A matter the townsfolk bring to you as the town grows. Some answers put a decree in force; some are remembered and come back in later stories.
What the town takes from households. Higher taxes fill the treasury but cost Mandate and put settlers off.
How well a god or a faction thinks of the town. Temples, shrines and patronage raise it; its blessings follow.
How much a secret faction has drawn the town's eye. High suspicion lets you crack down on it.
What a hero or a ward thinks of your choices. Every story choice shows who it would please or anger.
The town's weekly paper, once a printer sets up. You can pay for its front page, and heroes judge what you pay it to say.
A reward you post on a site in the wilds. A company takes it up when they think they can win. Only bounties the council pays for lift the fog from the map.

How a job is to be done: Slay clears a place for good, Drive off is quicker but something moves back in, Talk down bargains with clever foes, Fetch takes the hoard for the town. Heroes judge the terms you post.
A place in the wilds worth a bounty: a lair, a ruin, a dungeon. What lives there grows while nobody clears it.
Where monsters make their home. A lair you hear of but leave alone can fester into a named threat.
The map only shows what someone has told the town. Explorers, paid bounties, scrying and bought reports lift it.
Pay a company to wander a region. They report every lair, settlement, caravan or ruin they find and wait for your word on what to do.
Something explorers came on in the wilds. Investigate it chapter by chapter with d20 checks, or tell them to deal with it, move on or come home.
An hour's breather on the road: heroes bind wounds and catch their breath.
A night's sleep in camp: heroes heal fully and regain their spells, if the camp isn't attacked.
What heroes bring back. With loot terms or a loot pact, the hoard's magic goes to the town armory instead of the heroes.
The town hall's store of magic arms, armour and charms. Give them to heroes to help them take on harder sites.
A spoken message by magic. A party with a caster or a sending stone can ask you how to go on, and the game pauses for your answer.
Watching a far place by magic. Commission one from Bounties, or raise the Scrying Pool to see further.
Rangers posted to watch a site and report what moves there.
How many spells a caster can cast before a long rest. Sendings use them up.
How seasoned a hero or the mayor is. Higher levels mean more hit points, better rolls and harder sites they can take on.
The twenty-sided die. A check is a d20 roll plus a bonus from the roller's sheet, against a DC. A natural 20 always succeeds; a natural 1 always fails.
Difficulty Class: the number a d20 check has to meet or beat. The card shows your odds of making it.
A d20 roll plus a skill bonus against a DC: Persuasion to talk someone round, Athletics to haul or brawl, Insight to read a liar.
Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom and Charisma. Each skill rests on one of them.
Eighteen trained talents, from Athletics to Persuasion. Being trained or expert in one adds to its checks.
Earned by running the town well. Spend it on a story card to throw a failed roll again.
A special talent such as Lucky or Silver Tongue, taken at some levels instead of raising abilities.
Who someone was before: a soldier, a sage, a disgraced councillor. It decides which skills they are good at.
A person's abilities, skills and latest rolls. Everyone in town has one, and so do you.
Earned by seeing stories through. Enough of it gains a level.
Something happening in town you can step into. Each choice is a d20 roll of your own skill against a DC. Leave it alone and it runs its course without you.
What the town can put against an attack: the watch, heroes in town, a militia of townsfolk and the walls. Walls multiply it.
The town's paid guards. They patrol, stand at flags, catch thieves and man the walls when called to arms.
Townsfolk who take up arms when the town is attacked. They add to your defence, but fall more easily than the watch.
An order planted on the map (G): the nearest guards walk there and stand watch. Raiders shy away from what a flag covers.
Sends the nearest of the watch up onto a stretch of wall, a tower or the gate. A stretch with more guards than its share holds better.
A timber wall of sharpened stakes: the town's first defence, later replaced by stone walls.
Walls multiply your defence. Start with a palisade, then raise stone walls, a gatehouse, a moat and towers as the town grows.
Each adds to your defence, and its archers shoot when it is called to arms.
A portcullis over the main road. The gate holds better with one.
A ditch of water outside the walls that slows any assault.
Mercenary companies you hire for a fee and a daily wage. They stand on the walls and can march against a menace's holds. A company the treasury can't pay walks away.
A strike on the outlying farms. Raiders come when your heroes are away, and every raid they get away with makes them bolder.
A host marching on the town itself. Man the walls, call the watch to arms and bring heroes home.
Townsfolk carried off by raiders. Post a Rescue on the camp, or clear it, before their days run out.
Brass guards that never sleep and can't be bribed. They help catch a schemer's agents, but townsfolk don't like being watched by brass.
The first war: the warband's final march on the town. Win it and the wider wilds open.
The Bloodtusk orcs in the hills: the town's first enemy. They raid while your heroes are away and grow while their dungeons go uncleared, until they march.
A named enemy out in the land. A menace grows while nobody clears its seat, as far as its wits allow, and wants something: land, tribute, plague or your town.
The greatest foe of the campaign. A menace left to fester can become it. Only heroes can end it.
A menace's stronghold. Clear it and the menace breaks, falling back to a lair it holds.
How afraid the town is. Threats growing out in the land, razed settlements, raids and tribute raise it; victories bring it down.
Some enemies want the town kneeling. Bend the knee and pay tribute while their raiders stay away, or refuse and face their host.
Orc, goblin and giant warbands. They raid and burn, and want the lowland valleys for their own.
The dead who will not rest, often sworn to a fallen crown. They grow in winter, and want the living to kneel or join them.
Fiends, fey, hags and stranger things that buy towns one councillor at a time. Their agents work in secret; clockwork wardens and a straight watch catch them.
Monsters and great beasts. They hunt and spread, but have no greater plan.
Wyrms of the old Tyranny's blood. They take valleys as tribute and hoard what they take.
Secret faithful of dark powers, raising undead and fiends. They grow inside the town as well as out.
Robber barons and grasping traders who want the town's roads and coin.
The town's gods. A temple or shrine wins a god's favour, and its blessings follow.
A place of worship. Temples and shrines raise a god's favour and heal the sick.
A group taking root in town, open or secret. Back one with gold, or crack down on one that works against you.
A stretch of the land around the town with its own sites, peoples and dangers. The farther out, the deadlier.
Villages, dwarf holds, elf enclaves, free ports and oasis cities in the wilds. Each has a leader, its own adventurers and troubles. Help them and they remember.
Someone you send with gifts to win a settlement over.
What a settlement or company thinks of the town, from hostile to allied. Gifts, aid and caravans warm it; at 60 a people allies with you.
A caravan line to a friendly settlement. It sells your surplus and brings back what you are short of. Bigger charters run more routes.
What your scholars study in the library. Each town grows its own tree of discoveries from its trades, neighbours and institutions.
Books of spells from delves and caravans. They strengthen the library and open higher circles of town magic.
The old power an enemy, people or faction descends from, and what it still wants. The History screen tells each one's story.
The saga's chapters: Points of Light, The Wider Wilds, Lords of the Land and The Long Night. Each act opens wider and deadlier land.
Famous heroes and foes of your earlier towns. They can turn up again in a new campaign.
Icons along the top when something needs you: red is urgent, gold waits on your decision. Hover for a summary, click to go and answer it, right-click to dismiss.
The record of everything that happens in town, from brawls to weddings to dragons.
